Now *thalli* are the name given to vessels for offerings, which the priests used on the chief feasts, and they were shaped like towers [the Douay-Rheims takes *thalli* as 'boughs']. [[14:4|And that day indeed he held his peace|Et ipsa die siluit]] about the cause for which he had come, lest he should seem to have given the king gifts for his own advantage.

paras.t: Tempus autem opportunum dementiæ suæ nactus, id est consecutus ad aperiendum intentum insipientiæ ambitionisque suæ, convocatus a Demetrio ad consilium, etc. Ipsi qui dicuntur Assidæi Judæorum, id est inter Judæos assidue vacantes divinis, bella nutriunt, etc. Universæ accusationes hujus nequissimi Alcimi, sunt mendosæ. Sed oro, o rex, et regioni Judæorum, et generi, id est populo Judaico, secundum promulgatam omnibus humanitatem tuam, prospice, id est, provide de pace juxta tuam clementiam omnibus notam. Nam quamdiu superest Judas, id est eo vivente, impossibile est pacem esse negotiis Judæorum. Sic ambitiosi et fraudulenti suos ornant sermones, et prophetant non posse esse pacem in communitate, nisi hi qui ipsorum ambitioni resistunt, tollantur.
paras.en: [[14:5|But having gotten a convenient time to further his madness|Tempus autem opportunum dementiæ suæ nactus]], that is, having found it, to lay open the aim of his folly and ambition, [[14:5|being called to counsel by Demetrius|convocatus a Demetrio ad consilium]], etc.: [[14:6|They among the Jews that are called Assideans|Ipsi qui dicuntur Assidæi Judæorum]], that is, those among the Jews who are constantly (*assidue*) occupied with divine things, [[14:6|nourish wars|bella nutriunt]], etc. All the accusations of this most wicked Alcimus are lies. [[14:9|I beseech thee|Sed oro]], [[14:9|O king|o rex]], [[14:9|both of the country, and of our nation|et regioni Judæorum, et generi]], that is, the Jewish people, [[14:9|according to thy humanity which is known to all men|secundum promulgatam omnibus humanitatem tuam]] [the margin gives the Vulgate's *pervulgatam* beside Denis's *promulgatam*], [[14:9|take care|prospice]], that is, provide for peace according to thy clemency known to all. [[14:10|For as long as Judas liveth|Nam quamdiu superest Judas]], that is, while he lives, [[14:10|it is not possible that the state should be quiet|impossibile est pacem esse negotiis]] of the Jews. So do the ambitious and the deceitful adorn their speeches, and prophesy that there can be no peace in a community unless those who resist their ambition are taken away.

paras.t: Talibus autem ab hoc dictis, et ceteri amici Judæ ficti, vel amici Alcimi, hostiliter se habentes contra Judam, quem mendaciter accusabant, inflammaverunt Demetrium, id est ira, odio, indignatione adversus strenuissimum ac nobilissimum Judam. Dicit autem quidam hoc loco et alibi, quod licet Alcimus fuit de genere Aaron, non tamen descendit de eo per lineam sacerdotalem: quod non videtur posse salvari, nisi intelligatur de linea summi sacerdotii, quum in primo libro scribæ legantur dixisse de Alcimo, Homo sacerdos de semine Aaron venit. Qui statim Nicanorem misit in Judæam, etc.
paras.en: [[14:11|Now when this man had spoken to this effect|Talibus autem ab hoc dictis]], [[14:11|the rest also of the king's friends|et ceteri amici]], feigned friends of Judas, or friends of Alcimus, [[14:11|who were enemies of Judas|hostiliter se habentes contra Judam]], whom they lyingly accused, [[14:11|incensed Demetrius|inflammaverunt Demetrium]], that is, with anger, hatred and indignation against the most vigorous and most noble Judas. Now someone says in this place and elsewhere that although Alcimus was of the race of Aaron, yet he did not descend from him by the priestly line: which does not seem able to stand unless it is understood of the line of the high priesthood, since in the first book the scribes are read to have said of Alcimus: [[1 Mach 7:14|One that is a priest of the seed of Aaron is come|Homo sacerdos de semine Aaron venit]]. [[14:12|And forthwith he sent Nicanor|Qui statim Nicanorem misit]] [[14:12|into Judea|in Judæam]], etc.

paras.t: Audito Nicanoris adventu, Judæi conspersi terra: nam pro majore sui humiliatione superjecerunt capitibus suis terram, seu pulverem terræ; rogabant eum qui populum suum constituit, ut in æternum custodiret. Deus enim vult populum Judæorum manere usque in finem mundi, in quo et innumerabiles convertentur. Imperante autem duce, videlicet Machabæo, statim inde moverunt sui ad occurrendum Nicanori. Nicanor tamen audiens audaciam comitum, id est principum sociorumque, Judæ, etc., sanguine judicium facere metuebat, id est, per belli congressum non audebat exquirere, quis justiorem causam haberet, Judas an ipse Nicanor: ideo misit quosdam ad Judam pro amicitiis componendis. Et quum diu de his consilium ageretur a Juda et suis, et ipse dux ad multitudinem retulisset, id est, Judas causam hanc in generali sua convocatione proposuisset, omnium Judæorum fuit una sententia, amicitiis annuere, id est consensum præbere.
paras.en: [[14:15|Now when the Jews heard of Nicanor's coming|Audito Nicanoris adventu, Judæi]], [[14:15|they cast earth upon their heads|conspersi terra]]: for, to humble themselves the more, they threw earth, or the dust of the earth, upon their heads; [[14:15|and made supplication to him who chose his people to keep them for ever|rogabant eum qui populum suum constituit, ut in æternum custodiret]]. For God wills that the people of the Jews remain until the end of the world, in which countless of them will also be converted. [[14:16|Then at the commandment of their captain|Imperante autem duce]], namely Machabeus, [[14:16|they forthwith removed from the place where they were|statim inde moverunt]], his men, to go to meet Nicanor. [[14:18|Nevertheless Nicanor hearing of the valour of Judas's companions|Nicanor tamen, audiens virtutem comitum Judæ]] [Denis reads *audaciam*, 'boldness'; the margin gives the Vulgate's *virtutem*], that is, of his princes and comrades, etc., [[14:18|was afraid to try the matter by the sword|sanguine judicium facere metuebat]] [literally 'to make judgment by blood'], that is, he did not dare to find out by the clash of battle who had the juster cause, Judas or Nicanor himself: so [[14:19|he sent|misit quosdam]] certain men to Judas to make friendship. [[14:20|And when there had been a consultation thereupon|Et quum diu de his consilium ageretur]] by Judas and his men, [[14:20|and the captain had acquainted the multitude with it|et ipse dux ad multitudinem retulisset]], that is, Judas had put this matter before his general assembly, [[14:20|they were all of one mind|omnium Judæorum fuit una sententia]], [[14:20|to consent to covenants|amicitiis annuere]], that is, to give their consent.

paras.t: Morabatur autem Nicanor Jerosolymis, nihilque inique agebat contra Judæos. Fuit tamen idololatra, et impie agens contra Deum. Gregesque turbarum quæ congregatæ fuerant, id est, quas secum adduxerat ad pugnandum contra Judam, dimisit redire ad propria seu alia loca. Habebat autem Judam semper carum ex animo, et erat viro inclinatus. Rogavitque eum ducere uxorem, filiosque procreare. Nuptias fecit, etc. Verum de hac familiaritate et amicitia Judæ atque Nicanoris primo libro nil recitatur. Estque difficile hanc scripturam cum his, quæ in primo libro scripta sunt, concordare. Ibi enim legitur Demetrius misisse cum Alcimo Bacchidem, non Nicanorem, in primo accessu Alcimi ad ipsum Demetrium. Quumque Bacchides esset ad Demetrium regem reversus, et Alcimus non posset Judæ resistere, ad Demetrium rediit, qui tunc cum eo Nicanorem misit. Quumque Nicanor quasi decepisset Judam, conterritus est Judas, et amplius noluit videre faciem ejus, puta Nicanoris. Et post hoc commisit Nicanor prælium duplex contra Judam, sicut ibidem narratur. Hinc pro concordia videretur dicendum, quod prima vice Demetrius misit cum Alcimo Bacchidem atque Nicanorem; vel, quod hoc loco penitus subticetur primus accessus Alcimi ad Demetrium, et missio Bacchidis cum Alcimo in Judæam: et ita, quod dictum est hic de accessu Alcimi ad regem, intelligeretur de secundo accessu Alcimi ad regem Demetrium, et quod tunc cum Alcimo fuit missus Nicanor, qui semel contra Judam pugnavit, et postea cum eo ad tempus habuit pacem, sicut hic scribitur.
paras.en: [[14:23|And Nicanor abode in Jerusalem, and did no wrong|Morabatur autem Nicanor Jerosolymis, nihilque inique agebat]] against the Jews. Yet he was an idolater, and acted wickedly against God. [[14:23|but sent away the flocks of the multitudes that had been gathered together|gregesque turbarum quæ congregatæ fuerant, dimisit]], that is, those he had brought with him to fight against Judas, to return to their own or other places. [[14:24|And Judas was always dear to him from the heart, and he was well affected to the man|Habebat autem Judam semper carum ex animo, et erat viro inclinatus]]. [[14:25|And he desired him to marry a wife, and to have children|Rogavitque eum ducere uxorem, filiosque procreare]]. [[14:25|So he married|Nuptias fecit]], etc. But of this familiarity and friendship of Judas and Nicanor nothing is told in the first book. And it is hard to reconcile this scripture with what is written in the first book. For there we read that Demetrius sent Bacchides with Alcimus, not Nicanor, at Alcimus's first coming to Demetrius[[1 Mach 7:8||]]. And when Bacchides had gone back to King Demetrius, and Alcimus could not resist Judas, he returned to Demetrius, who then sent Nicanor with him[[1 Mach 7:25||]][[1 Mach 7:26||]]. And when Nicanor had as it were deceived Judas, Judas was terrified and would see his face, that is, Nicanor's, no more[[1 Mach 7:30||]]. And after this Nicanor fought two battles against Judas, as is told there[[1 Mach 7:31||]][[1 Mach 7:43||]]. Hence, to reconcile them, it would seem we must say that the first time Demetrius sent Bacchides and Nicanor with Alcimus; or that in this place the first coming of Alcimus to Demetrius, and the sending of Bacchides with Alcimus into Judea, are passed over altogether: and so what is said here of Alcimus's coming to the king would be understood of his second coming to King Demetrius, and that Nicanor was then sent with Alcimus, who fought once against Judas, and afterwards for a time had peace with him, as is written here.

paras.t: Alcimus autem videns caritatem illorum, scilicet Judæ et Nicanoris, ad invicem. Caritas hic extense sumitur pro amicitia sociali, non pro amore supernaturali infuso, quem certum est in Nicanore non fuisse. Venit ad Demetrium, et dicebat Alcimus Demetrio, Nicanorem rebus alienis, id est regi contrariis, assentire, communicando cum Juda. Sed quia regi resistere non poterat Nicanor, opportunitatem observabat qua præceptum perficeret, id est, quærebat capere Judam. Verumtamen non excusatur Nicanor a crimine, quod sic amicitiæ fœdus initum cum Juda, rupit. Imo magis debuit a Demetrio omnino recedere, quam ei in rebus ita illicitis obedire. At Machabæus videns austerius secum agere Nicanorem: quia per exteriora quædam indicia aversio Nicanoris patuit Judæ; occultavit se a Nicanore, non ex vituperanda formidine, sed ex prudentia et cautela. Ideo subditur: Quod cum ille, puta Nicanor, cognovit, fortiter, id est prudenter et virtuose, se a viro præventum, ita quod eum capere nequivit, dixit sacerdotibus: Nisi mihi Judam vinctum tradideritis, templum hoc Libero patri consecrabo, ita ut ad honorem Liberi seu Bacchi reædificetur. Asseruit enim Nicanor, quod templum combureret atque dejiceret.
paras.en: [[14:26|But Alcimus seeing the love they had one to another|Alcimus autem, videns caritatem illorum ad invicem]], namely of Judas and Nicanor. *Love* [*caritas*] is taken here broadly for the friendship of companions, not for the supernatural infused love, which it is certain was not in Nicanor. [[14:26|came to Demetrius|Venit ad Demetrium]], [[14:26|and told him that Nicanor|et dicebat Alcimus Demetrio, Nicanorem]] [[14:26|had assented|assentire]] [[14:26|to the foreign interest|rebus alienis]], that is, to things contrary to the king, by dealing with Judas. [[14:29|But because he could not oppose the king|Sed quia regi resistere non poterat]], Nicanor [[14:29|watched an opportunity to comply with the orders|opportunitatem observabat qua præceptum perficeret]], that is, sought to take Judas. Yet Nicanor is not excused from the crime of thus breaking the bond of friendship made with Judas. Rather he should have left Demetrius altogether than obey him in things so unlawful. [[14:30|But when Machabeus perceived that Nicanor was more stern to him|At Machabæus videns austerius secum agere Nicanorem]] (for by certain outward signs Nicanor's turning away became plain to Judas), [[14:30|hid himself from Nicanor|occultavit se a Nicanore]], not out of blameworthy fear, but out of prudence and caution. Therefore it follows: [[14:31|But he finding himself|Quod cum ille]], namely Nicanor, [[14:31|notably|fortiter]], that is, prudently and virtuously, [[14:31|prevented by the man|se a viro præventum]], so that he could not take him, [[14:31|commanded the priests|dixit sacerdotibus]]: [[14:33|Unless you deliver Judas prisoner to me|Nisi mihi Judam vinctum tradideritis]] [these words are damaged in the scan and are given as in the Vulgate], [[14:33|I will dedicate this temple to Bacchus|templum hoc Libero patri consecrabo]], so that it should be rebuilt in honour of Liber, or Bacchus. For Nicanor declared that he would burn the temple and cast it down.

paras.t: Razias autem quidam de senioribus, delatus, id est accusatus, est Nicanori tanquam zelator Judæ ac boni communis Judæorum; vir amator civitatis Jerusalem, cujus prosperitatem in temporalibus ac spiritualibus concupivit, ac pro viribus procuravit; et bene audiens, id est rationabiliter discernens quæ audiebat, indigentibus quoque benevolus; vel, Bene audiens, id est bene auditus a populo suo, sumendo activum pro passivo; qui pro affectu, id est propter caritatem suam ad populum suum, pater Judæorum appellabatur. Hic multis temporibus continentiæ propositum tenuit in Judaismo. Si per continentiam castitas designetur, potest dici quod mortua conjuge, de cetero castus permanserit. Per continentiam tamen potest intelligi generalis quædam virtutum conditio, scilicet moderantia seu repressio animi ab excessu. Corpusque et animam, id est vitam animalem, contentus tradere pro perseverantia, id est paratus dare in mortem pro virtutum constantia. Ad quem comprehendendum misit Nicanor. Putabat enim, si illum, scilicet Raziam, decepisset, id est, spiritualiter aut corporaliter occidisset, compellendo illum per pœnas ad paganismum, alioqui eum atrocissime trucidando, sese cladem maximam, id est miseriam et mœrorem gravissimum, Judæis illaturum, occiso spirituali et generali patre ipsorum. Qui quum jam comprehenderetur, id est, comprehendi quasi inciperet, gladio se petiit, id est percussit, eligens nobiliter potius mori, scilicet propria manu, ut hic insinuari videtur, quam subditus fieri peccatoribus, id est a gentilibus illis ad eorum voluntatem male tractari, et contra natales suos, id est ad progenitorum suorum irreverentiam, indignis injuriis agi, id est lædi.
paras.en: [[14:37|Now Razias, one of the ancients|Razias autem quidam de senioribus]], [[14:37|was accused to Nicanor|delatus est Nicanori]], that is, charged, as a zealot for Judas and for the common good of the Jews; [[14:37|a man that was a lover of the city|vir amator civitatis]] of Jerusalem, whose prosperity in temporal and spiritual things he desired and procured with all his strength; [[14:37|and of good report|et bene audiens]], that is, judging reasonably what he heard, kind also to the needy; or, *bene audiens*, that is, well heard of by his people, taking the active for the passive [*bene audiens*, literally 'hearing well', means 'well spoken of']; [[14:37|who for his kindness was called the father of the Jews|qui pro affectu pater Judæorum appellabatur]], that is, for his love for his people. [[14:38|This man, for a long time, had held fast his purpose of keeping himself pure in the Jews' religion|Hic multis temporibus continentiæ propositum tenuit in Judaismo]]. If by *continence* chastity is meant, it can be said that after his wife died he remained chaste thenceforward. But by continence can be understood a certain general condition of the virtues, namely the moderating or restraining of the mind from excess. [[14:38|and was ready to expose his body and life|corpusque et animam tradere contentus]], that is, his animal life, [[14:38|that he might persevere therein|pro perseverantia]], that is, ready to give it up to death for constancy in the virtues. And Nicanor sent men [[14:39|to take him|Ad quem comprehendendum]]. [[14:40|For he thought|Putabat enim]], if he had ensnared him, namely Razias, that is, killed him spiritually or bodily, by forcing him into paganism through punishments, or else by butchering him most cruelly, [[14:40|to hurt the Jews very much|sese cladem maximam, id est miseriam et mœrorem gravissimum, Judæis illaturum]], that is, bring very grievous misery and grief upon them, by slaying their spiritual and common father. [[14:41|when he was ready to be taken|Qui quum jam comprehenderetur]], that is, when they began as it were to seize him, [[14:41|he struck himself with his sword|gladio se petiit]], [[14:42|Choosing to die nobly|eligens nobiliter potius mori]], namely by his own hand, as seems to be suggested here, [[14:42|rather than to fall into the hands of the wicked|quam subditus fieri peccatoribus]], that is, to be ill-treated by those gentiles at their will, [[14:42|and to suffer abuses unbecoming his noble birth|et contra natales suos indignis injuriis agi]], that is, to the dishonour of his forefathers, that is, to be harmed.

paras.t: Videtur autem Augustinus in libro de Civitate Dei factum istud non commendare, et ad mollitiem asserit pertinere, se ipsum occidere ad evadendum graviora tormenta. Unde quod Samson se oppressit, et feminæ quædam sanctæ se ipsas submerserunt ne violarentur, ait non aliter excusari, nisi quod occulto Spiritus Sancti instinctu hoc egerint. Hebræi vero (ut fertur) dicunt licitum esse in duobus casibus, se ipsum occidere. Primo, ne quis acerbitate tormentorum ad infidelitatem trahatur. Secundo, ne in contemptum Dei vita sua ludibrio habeatur: et istud videtur auctor hujus libri sensisse. Dictum tamen Augustini, quod Glossa hic sequitur, et Thomas in secunda secundæ, aliique doctores communiter, verius esse censetur. Unde qui Raziam istum excusare omnino voluerit, dicere potest, quod occulto Dei instinctu sic fecerit. Postremo, in secunda secundæ de hac re scribit Thomas quæstione 64: Ad veram fortitudinem pertinet, non refugere mortem propter bonum commune; sed si quis sibi inferat mortem ut vitet mala pœnaliora, habet quamdam fortitudinis speciem (propter quod aliqui se ipsos occiderunt, æstimantes fortiter agere, de quorum numero fuit Razias); sed non est hoc vera fortitudo, sed quædam mollities animi dura perpeti non valentis, secundum Philosophum tertio Ethicorum, et Augustinum primo de Civitate Dei. Unde non licet se ipsum occidere ex timore consentiendi peccato: non enim sunt facienda mala ut proveniant bona, vel ut mala vitentur, præsertim quæ minora sunt et incerta.
paras.en: Augustine, in the book of the City of God, seems not to commend this deed, and asserts that to kill oneself to escape heavier torments belongs to softness. Hence he says that Samson's crushing himself[[Judg 16:30||]], and certain holy women's drowning themselves lest they be violated, cannot be excused otherwise than by their having done it at a hidden prompting of the Holy Ghost. The Hebrews (as is said) hold that it is lawful to kill oneself in two cases: first, lest one be drawn into unbelief by the bitterness of torments; secondly, lest one's life be made a mockery in contempt of God: and this the author of this book seems to have held. Yet the saying of Augustine, which the Gloss follows here, and Thomas in the *Secunda Secundæ*, and the other doctors commonly, is judged to be truer. So whoever wishes wholly to excuse this Razias can say that he did so at a hidden prompting of God. Lastly, Thomas writes of this matter in the *Secunda Secundæ*, question 64: It belongs to true fortitude not to shrink from death for the common good; but if someone inflicts death on himself to avoid more painful evils, he has a certain appearance of fortitude (for which reason some have killed themselves, thinking they acted bravely, and among their number was Razias); but this is not true fortitude, but rather a certain softness of a mind unable to bear hard things, according to the Philosopher in the third book of the Ethics, and Augustine in the first book of the City of God. Hence it is not lawful to kill oneself out of fear of consenting to sin: for evils are not to be done that good may come of them[[Rom 3:8||]], or that evils may be avoided, especially such as are lesser and uncertain.
